article_title: Evidence for ESSA: My Math Academy
citation: My Math Academy evidence summary. (2022). Age of Learning. https://www.ageoflearning.com/schools/systemcheck/
title: Adaptive game-based design combining scaffolding, embedded assessment, and narrative engagement
description: The program's design pattern combines a math curriculum with adaptive game-based learning: each game activity maps to a learning objective with "an interactive instruction level, as well as several layers of scaffolding and feedback." Adaptivity operates within games, between games, and across the system to give "a customized pathway between skills based on prior performance," with cohesive narrative and interactive characters supporting engagement.
requirements: Device compatibility with the program's minimum technical requirements
constraints: Designed for pre-kindergarten through second grade number sense and operations content
target_learners: Young children in pre-K through 2nd grade
examples: Game-based pretests and final assessment tasks at a granular skill level are embedded throughout the play experience
key_sources: My Math Academy evidence summary. (2022). Age of Learning. https://www.ageoflearning.com/schools/systemcheck/

article_title: A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents
citation: Seaton Eleanor K., Yip Tiffany, Sellers Robert M. (2009). A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2009.01268.x
title: Multidimensional Model of Racial Identity (MMRI): centrality and regard dimensions applied to adolescent discrimination research
description: The MMRI articulates individual differences in the meaning and significance African Americans ascribe to racial identity. The article states it "is comprised of four related dimensions, but only two are examined in the present study: centrality and regard". Racial centrality is the significance individuals place on race; regard divides into private regard (personal feelings about being African American) and public regard (beliefs about how broader society views African Americans). The study uses these dimensions to disaggregate which identity aspects respond to discrimination.
requirements: Measurement of the specific dimensions requires the Multidimensional Inventory of Black Identity adapted for youth (MIBI-T)
constraints: Only centrality and regard were examined; the other two MMRI dimensions were not tested in this study
target_learning_goals: Understanding how racial identity dimensions relate to experiences of racial discrimination over adolescence
examples: The study measured centrality, private regard and public regard with three items each from the MIBI-T across three annual waves
key_sources: Seaton Eleanor K., Yip Tiffany, Sellers Robert M. (2009). A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2009.01268.x

article_title: Revisiting Picture Functions in Multimedia Testing: A Systematic Narrative Review and Taxonomy Extension
citation: Schewior, L., & Lindner, M. A. (2024). Revisiting Picture Functions in Multimedia Testing: A Systematic Narrative Review and Taxonomy Extension. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09883-0
title: Four-function taxonomy of pictures in multimedia testing (decorative, representational, organizational, informational)
description: The review organizes pictures in test items by their functional relationship to the accompanying text, adapting Levin's MML classification. Decorative pictures "can be loosely associated with the item context but do not display task or solution relevant information"; representational pictures represent part or all of task-relevant text content; organizational pictures support the solution procedure by providing visuospatial structure; and informational pictures "depict information that is essential for the solution of the problem." The review uses this taxonomy to classify 62 studies and proposes simplification and extension in its discussion.
requirements: Pictures must be displayed simultaneously with the text-based problem statement or question in a testing context
constraints: The taxonomy was developed for multimedia testing contexts, not multimedia learning generally
Pictures in the same functional category can vary considerably in abstraction level
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of constructs in assessment
examples: The review classified 62 studies by picture function with high inter-rater reliability (Cohen's Kappa = 0.957)
key_sources: Schewior, L., & Lindner, M. A. (2024). Revisiting Picture Functions in Multimedia Testing: A Systematic Narrative Review and Taxonomy Extension. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09883-0

article_title: A Mixed-methods Study of How to Improve Primary-secondary Transitions in England: Combining Academic Research with Policy and Practice Consultation
citation: Bagnall, C. L., Edge, D., Banwell, E., Seymour, R., Garnett, N., Mason, C., Panayiotou, M., Jindal-Snape, D., Packer, R., Hodgkin, K., Skerritt, C., Donaldson, C., Birchwood, J., McAreavey, A., Cunningham, E., Symonds, J. E., & Holliman, A. (2026). A Mixed-methods Study of How to Improve Primary-secondary Transitions in England: Combining Academic Research with Policy and Practice Consultation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10174-z
title: Multiple and Multi-dimensional Transitions (MMT) theory frames primary-secondary transition as simultaneous changes across environment, social interactions, identity and academic expectations
description: The article draws on Jindal-Snape's Multiple and Multi-dimensional Transitions Theory to characterise the primary-secondary transition as a period in which "children navigate multiple simultaneous changes". Under MMT these include "transitions" in their school environment (including systemic structural, physical, and human aspects of change); social interactions (with both classmates and teachers); identity (primary/secondary school child, child/young person); and academic expectations. The article uses this lens to argue transitions should be examined through a multifaceted lens recognising interconnected changes for children and significant others in their ecosystem.
requirements: Examining transitions through a multifaceted lens that recognises the interconnected contribution of complex changes occurring for children and significant others within their ecosystem
target_learners: children around age 11 transitioning from primary to secondary school in England
target_learning_goals: emotional wellbeing and adjustment during school transitions
examples: The article applies MMT to frame its background section and the design of round-table questions across five ecological levels from pupil to national.

article_title: Surprise responses in the human brain demonstrate statistical learning under high concurrent cognitive demand
citation: Marta Isabel Garrido, Chee Leong James Teng, Jeremy Alexander Taylor, Elise Genevieve Rowe and Jason Brett Mattingley. (2016). Surprise responses in the human brain demonstrate statistical learning under high concurrent cognitive demand. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.6
title: MMN as a sensory prediction error marking implicit learning of probabilistic (non-rule-based) statistical structure
description: The framework treats the mismatch negativity — an early fronto-central response peaking at about 100–250 ms — as "a sensory prediction error and a neurophysiological marker of a learned regularity". The article extends classic oddball work to a probabilistic paradigm in which the regularity "can not be encoded as a deterministic sequence-based rule, a ﬁnite set of known stimuli, or by a categorical separation between expected and unexpected events". Learners implicitly encode the Gaussian distribution's variance, so prediction-error magnitude scales with a tone's improbability relative to its context. The article uses this framework to argue that change detection proceeds automatically even under cognitive demand.
requirements: Exposure to an auditory stream whose frequencies are sampled from a contextual distribution, with probe tones embedded to evoke prediction-error responses
constraints: Prediction-error generation likely combines release from adaptation with a second-order memory comparison mechanism; adaptation alone does not account for the responses
target_learning_goals: implicit learning of statistical regularities in the sensory environment
key_sources: Marta Isabel Garrido, Chee Leong James Teng, Jeremy Alexander Taylor, Elise Genevieve Rowe and Jason Brett Mattingley. (2016). Surprise responses in the human brain demonstrate statistical learning under high concurrent cognitive demand. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.6

article_title: Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation
citation: Zhao, L., Echeverria, V., Gašević, D., Yan, L., Alfredo, R., Li, X., & Martinez-Maldonado, R. (2026). Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation. Computers & Education, 252, 105655. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105655
title: MMLA system generating social and epistemic network visualisations of team communication in healthcare simulation
description: The article describes an AI-powered multimodal learning analytics system deployed in a nursing simulation space that captures audio and spatial data and automatically generates visualisations of team communication. The system "employs spatial analytics and a transformer-based language model (i.e., BERT) to process learners' physical positioning and speech data, enabling the visualisation of communication dynamics as Social and Epistemic Networks". Educators access a timeline and network interface on a tablet during debriefing and can select time spans to generate networks for specific phases.
requirements: Requires headset microphones, a Pozyx positioning toolkit for spatial coordinates and body orientation, and automated transcription with a fine-tuned BERT classifier for coding communication behaviours
constraints: The classifier was validated on a subset of the 2023 data (five sessions, approximately 10% of the data) with all Cohen's κ > 0.61
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing learners in simulation-based clinical courses
target_learning_goals: Reflection on collaboration and closed-loop communication
examples: Deployed across 63 simulations involving 252 learners in a third-year undergraduate clinical course, with five clinical educators leading debriefings
key_sources: Zhao, L., Echeverria, V., Gašević, D., Yan, L., Alfredo, R., Li, X., & Martinez-Maldonado, R. (2026). Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation. Computers & Education, 252, 105655. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105655

article_title: A systematic review of comprehensive Robotic-assisted surgical (RAS) curricula.
citation: Kieslich Anna K., Jardine Ruari, Ibrahim Hussain, Calvert Areeg, Walker Kenneth G., Walker Kim A., Watson Angus J. M. (2026). A systematic review of comprehensive Robotic-assisted surgical (RAS) curricula. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02962-6
title: The Modified Medical Education Research Study Quality Instrument (MMERSQI) for assessing study quality in medical education research.
description: The MMERSQI is a tool for assessing the quality of studies in medical education research, used in this review with a minimum score of 23.5 and a maximum score of 100. The review reports that "The modified MERSQI scoring does not differentiate between descriptive statistics or simple inferential statistics" and that "Points are doubled when modelling is used." The review used this tool to assess the methodological quality of the included studies, finding overall low quality.
requirements: The tool requires a distinction between descriptive statistics, simple inferential statistics, and complex modelling, which the review notes is not clearly defined in the MMERSQI publication.
constraints: The modified MERSQI scoring does not differentiate between descriptive statistics or simple inferential statistics.
key_sources: Kieslich Anna K., Jardine Ruari, Ibrahim Hussain, Calvert Areeg, Walker Kenneth G., Walker Kim A., Watson Angus J. M. (2026). A systematic review of comprehensive Robotic-assisted surgical (RAS) curricula. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02962-6

article_title: Enhancing Direct Instruction on Introductory Physics for Supporting Students' Mental-Modeling Ability
citation: Mansyur, J., & Darsikin. (2016). Enhancing Direct Instruction on Introductory Physics for Supporting Students' Mental-Modeling Ability. International Education Studies, 9(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n6p32
title: MMA rubric (Wang 2007, modified by Mansyur 2010) for scoring mental-modeling ability
description: A rubric used to assess students' mental-modeling ability, with components scored to a maximum total of 12: generating a mental model with and without a 2D representation (1a/1b), manipulating the mental model based on propositions or possessing a rigid model (2a/2b), metacognitive monitoring, and self-checking with an alternative approach. The article states, "MMA rubric was predominantly used to assess Component 1a (or 1b) and 2a (or 2b) of Table 1 as the main focus of this study." Components 3 and 4 were not included in this article.
requirements: Test problems containing elements as a stimulus for students to use a diagram in problem-solving activity
Counting multiple diagrams per problem as one, giving a maximum of five diagrams per student
constraints: Components 3 (metacognitive monitoring) and 4 (self-checking) are marked as not included in this article
target_learners: Introductory physics students at university level
target_learning_goals: Generating and manipulating mental models based on propositions and representations
examples: Applied to pretest and posttest essay answers on Kinematics, Dynamics, and Work-Energy in both experimental and control groups
key_sources: Mansyur, J., & Darsikin. (2016). Enhancing Direct Instruction on Introductory Physics for Supporting Students' Mental-Modeling Ability. International Education Studies, 9(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n6p32

article_title: Teaching Medical Students to Help Patients Manage Their Weight: Outcomes of an Eight-School Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Ockene JK, Pbert L, Crawford S, Frisard CF, Pendharkar JA, Sadasivam RS, Faro J, Okuliar C, Eno C, Margo K, Shaw MA, Soleymani T, Stadler DD, Warrier S, White K, Geller AC. (2021). Teaching Medical Students to Help Patients Manage Their Weight: Outcomes of an Eight-School Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of General Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-020-06571-x
title: Multi-modal education framework guided by Social Cognitive Theory and Socio-Ecological Theory
description: The MSWeight intervention is "a multi-modal educational intervention (MME) guided by Social Cognitive Theory, and Socio-Ecological Theory", designed to address key theoretical constructs at the individual, interpersonal, and institutional levels hypothesized to influence weight management counseling skills. The web course targets attitudes, the role-play and standardized web-patient encounter provide practice and structured feedback, and preceptor-facilitated clerkship teaching provides observation, instruction, and feedback, together intended to build skills and reinforce confidence.
requirements: Curriculum elements operating at individual, interpersonal, and institutional levels together, hypothesized to provide a structured foundation for building and practicing skills
constraints: The framework was hypothesized rather than directly tested; the trial found few MME-versus-TE differences on skills outcomes
examples: The web course is intended to help students develop positive attitudes toward WMC; the role-play exercise and web-patient encounter provide practice and structured feedback
key_sources: Ockene JK, Pbert L, Crawford S, Frisard CF, Pendharkar JA, Sadasivam RS, Faro J, Okuliar C, Eno C, Margo K, Shaw MA, Soleymani T, Stadler DD, Warrier S, White K, Geller AC. (2021). Teaching Medical Students to Help Patients Manage Their Weight: Outcomes of an Eight-School Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of General Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-020-06571-x

article_title: Exploring sociodemographic subgroup differences in multiple mini-interview (MMI) performance based on MMI station type and the implications for the predictive fairness of the Hamburg MMI.
citation: Knorr M, Meyer H, Sehner S, Hampe W, Zimmermann S. (2019). Exploring sociodemographic subgroup differences in multiple mini-interview (MMI) performance based on MMI station type and the implications for the predictive fairness of the Hamburg MMI. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1674-z
title: Station type as a design feature that determines which constructs an MMI assesses and which subgroup differences can be expected
description: The article proposes that MMI station types tap different constructs: simulation stations involve direct interaction with a simulated patient and "respond to the emotions displayed by the actor (i.e., affective empathy)", interview stations tap "cognitive processes such as perspective taking (i.e., cognitive empathy) and self-reflection", and group stations measure teamwork skills combining leadership, collective problem solving and team orientation. On this framework, subgroup differences (e.g., the female advantage at simulation and interview stations but not group stations) can be related to the dimensions assessed and interpreted as narrow evidence for validity rather than as bias.
requirements: Station developers must align station type with the dimensions they intend to assess, since station type is "one of the most basic and controllable aspect of MMI design"
constraints: The authors state their results allow no definite conclusion that simulation stations assess affective empathy and interview stations measure perspective taking; they suggest classifying stations by the degree to which they require affective versus cognitive empathy for a stronger test
target_learning_goals: psychosocial competencies including empathy, self-reflection and teamwork
examples: The Hamburg MMI assesses psychosocial competencies via simulation and interview stations since 2010, with two group stations added in 2016 to assess teamwork skills
key_sources: Knorr M, Meyer H, Sehner S, Hampe W, Zimmermann S. (2019). Exploring sociodemographic subgroup differences in multiple mini-interview (MMI) performance based on MMI station type and the implications for the predictive fairness of the Hamburg MMI. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1674-z

article_title: Detecting Mistakes in CPR Training with Multimodal Data and Neural Networks.
citation: Di Mitri Daniele, Schneider Jan, Specht Marcus, Drachsler Hendrik. (2019). Detecting Mistakes in CPR Training with Multimodal Data and Neural Networks. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s19143099
title: MMLA Pipeline — an open-source workflow for collection, storage, annotation, analysis and exploitation of multimodal learning data
description: The Multimodal Learning Analytics Pipeline [36] is "a workflow for the collection, storage, annotation, analysis and exploitation of multimodal data for supporting learning". The study used three open-source components: the Multimodal Learning Hub for synchronised multi-sensor recording into MLT session files, the Visual Inspection Tool for manual and semi-automatic annotation of psychomotor tasks, and the MLT data format storing time-synchronised sensor JSON plus video. The authors believe the method "can be used as road map for the general identification of learners mistakes using multimodal data in authentic training procedures".
requirements: Manual synchronisation of annotation files with sensor recordings, aided by sensor data plots and video in the VIT
Intensive data geology steps to obtain meaningful interpretations, as multimodal data are messy
constraints: No standardised procedures exist in the field, so the pipeline is an emerging approach
target_learners: Researchers building multimodal tutoring systems for psychomotor learning
target_learning_goals: Automatic detection of learner mistakes in physical-skill training
examples: Each two-minute CPR session was saved as a 17 Mb MLT file with Kinect JSON, Myo JSON and an MP4 recording; annotations were synced with manual time offsets
key_sources: Di Mitri Daniele, Schneider Jan, Specht Marcus, Drachsler Hendrik. (2019). Detecting Mistakes in CPR Training with Multimodal Data and Neural Networks. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s19143099

article_title: Detecting Mistakes in CPR Training with Multimodal Data and Neural Networks.
citation: Di Mitri Daniele, Schneider Jan, Specht Marcus, Drachsler Hendrik. (2019). Detecting Mistakes in CPR Training with Multimodal Data and Neural Networks. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s19143099
title: Two approaches to multimodal learning analytics: the analytics approach and the modelling approach
description: The article distinguishes two approaches within MMLA: "(1) the 'analytics' approach which aims at presenting insights to the educational actors, helping them to provide a better feedback, particularly useful in ill-structured learning tasks; and (2) the 'modelling' approach, used also by the ITS community, which aims at using machine learning to automatically classify or predict learning dimensions". Examples that combine the two suggest a continuum between the ITS and MMLA fields rather than a black-and-white division. The Multimodal Tutor for CPR exemplifies the modelling approach, and the authors note its data can support both automatic feedback and retrospective human feedback.
requirements: Machine learning classifiers need annotated performance-indicator labels as classification targets
constraints: The modelling approach is described in the MMLA literature via the Multimodal Learning Analytics Model (MLeAM), cited rather than developed here
target_learners: Researchers and designers of multimodal learning analytics systems
target_learning_goals: Detecting learner mistakes and predicting learning dimensions from multimodal data
examples: The CPR study's classifiers instantiate the modelling approach; dashboards and data-storytelling instantiate the analytics approach
key_sources: Di Mitri Daniele, Schneider Jan, Specht Marcus, Drachsler Hendrik. (2019). Detecting Mistakes in CPR Training with Multimodal Data and Neural Networks. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s19143099
